newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria hopes to continue free AIDS treatment.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria hopes to continue free AIDS treatment.

text.p: Bulgaria's health ministry said on Thursday it was short of funds for AIDS education campaigns but would do its best to continue free treatment to patients despite the economic crisis.
Deputy Health Minister Radka Argirova told a news conference Bulgaria had registered 185 people as HIV positive since 1986 and 43 people had died of AIDS.

"We will do our best to secure free medication but we also look forward to developing contacts with international organisations and possibly receiving some financial support from United Nations missions and the World Bank," she said.
A six-month treatment with the drug AZT costs 500,000 levs (currently about $1,400) per patient and the ministry also spends some $216,000 annually on HIV tests.

A strict monetary regime expected to be introduced early next year to halt the collapse of the lev will oblige Bulgaria to present a balanced budget, which diplomats and economists say will mean big cuts in public spending. Spending this year is already 20 percent over budget targets.
Argirova said 128 of those diagnosed as HIV positive had acquired the virus through heterosexual contact. The first cases were among Bulgarian sailors infected overseas, she said.
She said another problem was the stigma attached to the disease and doctors' reluctance to take on the task of treating HIV-infected patients.

"We need to provide additional training to doctors to change their attitude to the AIDS problem as at this stage most regional doctors prefer to send all their HIV-positive patients to the Infectious Disease Centre in Sofia," Argirova said.

She said four of those known to have been infected were drug addicts, 17 had acquired the virus through homosexual contacts, 14 were haemophilics and four had been given infected blood through transfusions.

The health ministry plans to submit a draft national anti-AIDS programme to the goverment, and will start compulsory classes on safe sex and family planning in secondary schools, but Argirova complained she lacked the funds for condom distribution programmes.
In 1996 the health ministry gave 300,000 levs to support safe-sex promotion campaigns of non-governmental organisations.
A Bulgarian firm, Cross-M Ltd, began producing Sport brand condoms this year in the town of Byala.
